items.label: text
items.text: potassium hydroxide but are not so sure of the concentration of the dilute hydrochloric acid solution (the label has gone missing!). The following method could be used to find out the concentration of the acid and how much heat is released during the neutralisation reaction.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Place a polystyrene cup in a 250 cm³ glass beaker.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Transfer 25 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ potassium hydroxide into the polystyrene cup using a measuring cylinder.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Record the initial temperature.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Fill a burette with 50.00 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Use the burette to add 5.00 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid to the potassium hydroxide.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Stir vigorously and record the maximum temperature reached.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Continue adding further 5.00 cm³ portions of dilute hydrochloric acid to the cup, stirring and recording the maximum temperature each time, until a total volume of 50.00 cm³ has been added.

items.label: text
items.text: We can plot a graph of the temperature of the mixture versus the volume of acid added.

items.label: text
items.text: In this reaction the temperature increases at first but then decreases. The reaction between the acid and the alkali is exothermic. At the beginning the temperature goes up because the acid reacts with the alkali, giving out heat. But when all the alkali has been used up, we are just adding cold acid to our warm solution (there is no reaction because there is nothing for the acid to react with)and the temperature goes down.

items.label: text
items.text: Two lines of best fit can be drawn on our graph. The point where the lines cross represents complete neutralisation. From the graph, we can identify the maximum temperature reached during the experiment as 31.8 °C. At this point, 28.00 cm³ of acid has been used.

items.label: text
items.text: To work out how much heat is released in the neutralisation reaction, we can To work out how much heat is released in the neutralisation reaction, we can use the same calculation as before.

items.label: text
items.text: The total volume of the solution at the neutralisation point is 25 + 28 = 53 cm³.

items.label: text
items.text: Heat given out is shown by Q = mc∆T = 53 × 4.18 × (31.8 - 19.3) = 2769.3J.

items.label: text
items.text: If we divide by 1000we get 2.7693 kJ.

items.label: text
items.text: Here we assume the following:

items.label: list_item
items.text: The density of the reaction mixture is the same as that of water, so 1 cm³ of solution has a mass of 1 g.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The specific heat capacity of the mixture is the same as that of water. This is a fairly reasonable assumption because the neutralised solution is mostly water.

items.label: text
items.text: Now we need to calculate how much heat is released when 1 mole of potassium hydroxide reacts with 1 mole of hydrochloric acid:
